title: Engineering, ethics and our common future
text:
The 2026 world cup ended with Spain taking la copa mundial. Kudos to everyone who participated. As I write, there has been a train collision between a high-speed train with a stationary train near Toledo in Spain. This is the third train crash this year in Spain.
All this without it being related made think about engineering, ethics and our common future. Everything is related.
What things we are called to deliver well as engineers! What more could lie in the immense panorama and rubble that we have around? We constantly need to look at details, understand load paths from roof to foundation. A while ago, I met a gentleman, who asked me what book it was I was holding. It was a book by Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics. Upon noticing it was on ethics, he asked what I do in life “structural engineering practice,” I retorted. He immediately argued “Engineers do not need ethics. Leave it for those in public life, politics, lawyers, and the humanities.” We parted with broad smiles. This got me thinking.
I have experienced odd moments, read stories near and far, on events in the construction industry. We are aware of the escapades that take place daily; from how business is secured through the tendering process, to how profits are made even at the cost of significant compromises on integrity of materials used, or some processes and procedures, or how clients take their sweet time paying for designs or works, if they pay. This is from multi-billion projects to easy backyard works. They tell the story of man – capable of the good, the bad and ugly all at the same time.
As is obvious, in all fields of human activity, whether economics, engineering, psychology, and sociology, and biology, ethics plays an inherent and indispensable role. That simple idea of “do the good, avoid the evil” is an impetus to all activity. Every human action has in the first consideration, an end. We always act to obtain something. And for us, the end does not justify the means. In fact, the end determines the means.
To divert briefly, as we well know, engineering comes from the Latin word, ingenium, which refers to our creative and designing faculty: the genius. Engineers develop a rigorous background of science and mathematics, which they use with other technical skills. Since an engineer’s work is human action, which he can neglect or fulfil, do well or do poorly, and benefit or hurt his family based on where his work priorities fall, ethics most certainly plays a role in that work; an engineer must take ethics into account.
Everything is related, nothing happens in isolation. For us to improve ethics in the construction industry, a series of items need to be put in proper order. Mostly, it is a question of each one’s contribution. If our leaders be corrupt, it is only a reflection of the society from which they hail. This simply means “I” am corrupt, period. And it is really up to me to propose a better narrative.
Our common future will be shaped by ideals that go beyond us. And like every revolution, it takes relentless stubbornness to do one’s best to sail against the tide. And yet, we recognise that this is worthwhile. We engineers, like everyone else, have a unique responsibility to the community, and in addition to the codes of ethics which help to define the space within which we play to secure the good of all, our better judgement, fostered by a sharpened capacity to see, will go a long way in securing a better world.

title: Engineering, ethics and our common future
section: The whole is greater than sum of its parts
text:
The whole is greater than sum of its parts
We always remember that the whole is always greater than the sum of its parts. The joints of a building are important, and need to be adequate for the forces that will be transferred through them. Nevertheless, the building’s function as a whole is even more important. We live in extraordinary times, times where we have technology to harness. And it is easy to bypass firewalls if we know how. We need a deeper ethical imperative, perhaps, we could re-write history with more stories of ethical leadership and business in the sector of infrastructure.
The action of structural engineers LeMessurier in the aftermath of the Citicorp Building in New York, is a bold testament of professional ethical conduct. If we do not yet know the story, an easy Google search will suffice. We need more actions like these. We need some more rigor and iterations in the designs we propose, sometimes, not being afraid to ask around for opinions, so that economy and good engineering sense thrive. Not that we should get stuck in the mud with a billion iterations. Rather, that we get prudent as we go along.
And forward, we look to equipping better skills, with lectures that are attended by both students and professors timely, with better laboratories, and a relentless effort to think global, so as to compete global. Oh, and that important gem – continuous professional development, not being afraid to learn, or better being courageous enough to learn. How many of us are still using the same ancient design software, and books that we had in our undergraduate studies, or some spreadsheets that obviously always work? BIM is around for example, a bit pricey, but worth investing in it, for doing some integrated designs simultaneously.
I used to get caught in traffic in Nairobi and Kampala, like everyone else, the world over. And one begins to wonder why we do not yet have a diverse transport system. Why not trams, trains, for example? Or something significantly. Travel to many countries, and you will notice the better planning. Why not in our pat of the world?
The task ahead, of cultivating a society that honours the common good, is necessary and urgent. We engineers and all players in the built environment, are invaluable along this adventure, We, all of us, should reach the point of saying, behind our religious convictions and the diversity of our cultural, and professional presuppositions, what are the fundamental values for our common humanity, in a manner to work together to promote comprehension, reciprocal recognition and peaceful cooperation between all the members of the human family.

title: Engineering, ethics and our common future
text:
Para pro futuro
Is it realistically possible to run an engineering/construction business bila magendo? Of course, it is. Though tough and tricky with the cartels, and sharks all over the place, and even more so in our multicultural world, it is possible. We recognise the importance of efforts to channel resources to the good of society, guided by a premise. And if we do, can we dare to do things differently? Whether things can change is fairly obvious, whether they will, is a more real question. Depends on you, depends on me. Albert Einstein suggested “Insanity: doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.” We need some significant insanity to set the ship to sail in the direction we know is better than what we have. The Uganda Institution of Professional Engineers has as its motto, Para pro futuro, Prepare for the future. And for the future we design and build, and we do so ethically, no? You are right, yeah, ethically! Suppose we decided to for gold in the arena of ethical engineering?

title: About
text:
We are a structural engineering practice born in Nairobi in 2019. Now based in Kampala, Uganda, we collaborate on timber projects across East Africa.
In March 2025, we began winding down active operations and stopped accepting new business. We handed over our final project in April 2026, completing our transition into a strategic pause. This pause allows us to focus on structural timber research and deepen our engineering understanding of timber as a key structural building material, within a local context.
We remain available for queries regarding our past work. Our doors going forward are wide open for timber-related collaborations. Sure, bring them on, we are game.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
The Built by Nature Summit 2026 was held in Barcelona—the 2026 World Capital of Architecture—with underlying pursuits on how to deliver housing at scale while staying within planetary boundaries. How can we continue Housing the World, without Costing the Earth?
Between 5 and 6 October 2026, I had the joy of participating in this annual summit. It is easy to see the immense value in networks, sharing knowledge, and meeting people dedicated to this cause.
Arriving from Madrid on a train just after 12 noon, I received a notice that the event opening would be delayed by half an hour due to a Generalitat de Catalunya advisory limiting non-essential movement before 14:00h. This was due to heavy rain and flood warnings—mindful of the recent severe flooding in Valencia that caused so many challenges for local communities.
Noticeably, friends and participants from the Netherlands were numerous from every corner. Keep it up, friends!

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
Bio-based materials and context
For some reason, although several bio-based materials exist (bamboo, hemp, straw), timber always seems to take center stage in the bio-based construction conversation. As part of teh summit, the day two city tour around Barcelona which centered on timber bear witness to this. Perhaps it is because of its potential for industrialisation, scaling, structured utilisation, and organized, traceable supply chains.
Bamboo grows in weeks—wow! Kudos to those driving its development for construction.
An underlying theme throughout the summit was the need to maintain evidence while keeping solutions firmly within their socio-economic and environmental context. If hybrid construction with timber gets us further, let us go for it! The idea is to try to build more with nature.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
The timber truth
A subtle but very evocative moment during the summit sparked a modest resolution: to start sharing—even in the most imperfect way—stories, lessons, challenges, and dreams around timber for the good of East Africa.
At a specific point, I found myself standing in front of Tamara Streefland (Built by Nature Head of Programme) and Peter King (Built by Nature CEO). I asked them for the price of The Timber Truth by Pablo van der Lugt. Both in unison simply replied:






NoteTwo generous friends



Well friend, there is this copy in front of us [lying on a chair] you can take it. — Tamara and Peter


Tamara and Peter did not realize it, but a tear or two of gratitude dropped from my eyes for this gesture of generosity and kindness. I figured right then that I should do something about the dreams I hold around a built environment that works in harmony with nature for Uganda, my beloved land, and for East Africa. To try to also give, and be more generous sharing information, stories.
Often, we can feel a little alone when trying to make sense of our efforts against the demands of keeping a practice going, paying those we employ, and balancing our commitments to family and friends.
This book, The Timber Truth, treats many wonderful themes, dismantles false premises, and tells accurate stories about the role of timber in the built environment. Its contents cover structural quality and performance, environment and climate, forestry and availability, and market economics.
As a personal rhythm, I hope to write something whenever family life and work deliverables allow—modest contributions published on this website to add to the existing body of knowledge around timber in the built environment in East Africa. Little by little, sharing resources, tools, and ideas that might help someone someday.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
Connections across the sector
Without trying to remotely exhaust the list of attendees and the various organisations they represented, I personally remember meeting people from: Wood Knowledge Wales, Bauhaus Earth, CSFEP, IAAC, Built by Nature, FSC, Stora Enso, Egoin Wood, WTA UK (who won the Built by Nature Frontrunner of the Year award), Ahora Madera, SUMA Arquitectura, Kenya National Housing Corporation, Green Building Council Kenya, Gatsby Africa, Timberworld Kenya, Lotino Engineering, Batlleiroig, and SHOUT Africa.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
Barcelona city tours
Day two was filled with site tours around Barcelona, visiting various projects split across different groups. My group had the joy of touring the Batlleiroig HQ, Sant Joan de Déu Medicine Centre and after a wonderful lunch (thanks to the organisers!) finally ended with a visit to Real Club de Polo de Barcelona.
The last site visit was at a local sports facility—incredible and beautiful. Realising I had a train back to Madrid at 16:25h when it was already 14:43h left little time to return to my hotel (requiring 50 minutes on the metro) and get back to Estació de Sants (another 40 minutes). I basically needed to run between locations. I did all this (and prayed too, duh!) and arrived within 10 minutes of the train closing its doors. Thanks to teh adrenaline. I started writing this article during the train leaving Barcelona.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
text:
Researching structural timber — for Uganda
Since 8 September, I have been focusing more on structural timber as a specific point of investigation. I am not sure where this journey will take me, but I hope it serves Uganda and East Africa toward a cost-effective approach to fulfilling the deep desire people have to own their own home as a form of freedom. Timber could be a viable option for many.
My backdrop remains Uganda—the Pearl of Africa. During the guided tour, one of the hosts mentioned she had visited Uganda and promised to share her story later in the visit. Sadly, I could not wait, as I had to run to catch the train.
A phrase from Pablo’s book that stuck with me is “from forest to frame.” As a structural engineer, it reminded me that I am loosely responsible for the frame end of that journey. Is it optimal? Is it safe against whatever could be thrown at it, including fire?
On the forest side, we seem to maintain a sufficient FSC supply (such as Busoga Forestry in Uganda) that can be utilized. Strength grading, of course, belongs as a core responsibility of the sawmilling process—sending a predictable grade and quality to market. Currently, this isn’t happening consistently, perhaps because the market does not yet demand it. Furthermore, building codes across Uganda, Kenya, and East Africa remain a little too rudimentary or too simple on timber design.
I was also surprised by a detail shared by a Spanish architect: in Spanish public procurement law, the design team (architects, engineers) is not allowed to interact with contractors or builders prior to formal contract award. This is tricky for the timber world, where all parties are often learning together. Jumping on the drawing board together early makes life so much easier and more efficient.

title: Housing the world, without costing the earth
section: While on the train from Barcelona to Madrid
text:
While on the train from Barcelona to Madrid
Writing on the train between Barcelona and Madrid, travelling at operational speeds between 190 km/h and 250 km/h (hitting 300 km/h on specific stretches along the 621-kilometre high-speed line), I hope I live to see reliable rail connections across Uganda and Africa. It would transform business, livelihoods, and regional integration—not just timber construction. It requires long-term order and a plan that spans political regimes, respected and invested in consistently for the common good.
During the summit, I met Marianne, a Dutch professional working in quality management who focuses on connecting interests to see how systems function as a whole. I found this thought rich and beautiful: How does everything function as a whole?

Thanks to the organisers, and to everyone who participated. Let us continue in our own way building by nature where possible. You can find more details about the event on the official Built by Nature 2026 Summit Page.
I dream that timber will become an important material choice for construction in Uganda, and I hope to work alongside many others to see that day come true. Oh Uganda, may God uphold thee.
